item.title: BRICS summit gives boost to Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BRICS summit gives boost to Global South High-quality cooperation, solidarity strengthened, foreign minister says The BRICS summit in New Delhi strengthened common ground among major Global South countries on development, cooperation, multilateralism and global governance reform amid global volatility and recurring regional conflicts, officials and analysts said as President Xi Jinping concluded a two-day visit to India on Sunday. The summit, which brought Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi together for their third consecutive year of bilateral talks, also gave fresh impetus to improving relations between the two neighbors, with broader implications for regional stability and Global South cooperation, they said. Speaking to reporters upon the conclusion of Xi's visit, Foreign Minister Wang Yi described the trip as a major diplomatic engagement with Global South countries in the opening year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period. Coming after Xi's visits to Central Asia and the Middle East earlier this month, the trip was strategically significant for advancing high-quality cooperation within the expanded BRICS grouping and strengthening Global South solidarity, Wang said. In less than 24 hours in the Indian capital, Xi attended nearly 10 events, discussed development and cooperation with BRICS leaders, and held in-depth talks with Modi to chart the course of bilateral relations, Wang said. This year marks the 20th anniversary of BRICS cooperation. At the summit, Xi said solidarity and cooperation had always been the source of the grouping's strength. He called on BRICS countries to take a leading role in innovation-driven development, safeguarding peace and stability, promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations, and reforming and improving global governance. At a new historical juncture, Xi had responded to the high expectations of Global South countries by reaffirming the historic mission of BRICS cooperation and charting its future course, Wang said, noting that Xi's urging elevated the strategic importance of BRICS cooperation and bolstered members' resolve and confidence to seek strength through solidarity. Speaking at a media briefing on Saturday, Sudhakar Dalela, secretary for economic relations at India's Ministry of External Affairs, said that there was a broad convergence among BRICS leaders on the need to strengthen multilateralism and to make global governance institutions more representative, inclusive, effective and responsive to today's realities. To bolster the strength of the Global South, Xi said during the summit that Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, hold high the banner of multilateralism, remain committed to a people-centered development philosophy and jointly advance security governance. He proposed five initiatives for "greater BRICS" cooperation in artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, intelligent manufacturing and talent development. Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at National University of Singapore's Business School, said "greater BRICS" distinguished itself through concrete plans to benefit people in countries beyond its membership. "The BRICS summit has a broader implied message for the international community — global development cannot be based on a zero-sum game mentality where development is pursued at the expense of others," he said. Swaran Singh, a former professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, India, said that Xi had presented "greater BRICS" as a platform for a more multipolar, rules-based order, with a strong emphasis on practical cooperation. He said Xi's proposals overlapped significantly with India's own emphasis on technology, resilient supply chains and a stronger role for the Global South in shaping international affairs. With China set to assume BRICS' rotating presidency for the fourth time next year, Wang said the country would remain committed to, rooted in and supportive of the Global South, sharing opportunities and pursuing common development on the path toward modernization. The bilateral meeting between Xi and Modi, following their talks in the Russian city of Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin in northern China in 2025, also brought the direction of China-India relations into focus. Wang said the two leaders held candid, in-depth exchanges on strategic and long-term issues shaping bilateral relations, with their most important consensus being that China and India should be partners. Under the leaders' strategic guidance, ties have gradually emerged from a low point, with an expanding range of cooperation, record bilateral trade and more active people-to-people exchanges, Wang said. Improved relations serve the interests of the two countries' more than 2.8 billion people and are also important for strengthening Global South cooperation, he added. India's Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement on Saturday that the leaders welcomed the steady progress in relations since their Tianjin meeting and reaffirmed the need to take a strategic and long-term perspective on the bilateral ties. "Differences should not become disputes," the statement said. Wang said that each country's development offers opportunities for the other, and that China-India cooperation has significance far beyond bilateral ties, with implications for the Global South and the world as a whole. He urged both sides to build on the hard-won improvement and implement the leaders' consensus to contribute to regional and global peace and prosperity.

item.title: Nation's smart computing scale surges
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Nation's smart computing scale surges China Mobile building AI data centers, deploying gigawatt-level parks China has achieved integrated, coordinated monitoring of computing power nationwide, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced during the recent 2026 China Computational Power Conference in Langfang, Hebei province, as the country accelerates construction of a unified national computing network. By end-June, China's intelligent computing scale reached 2,185 EFLOPS, or exa floating-point operations per second, up 177 percent year-on-year. More than 70 computing transmission channels linking computing hubs and key regions have been built, and 17 regional nodes for national computing interoperability have been approved, it was noted at the conference, which concluded on Sunday. He Baohong, chief engineer of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, or CAICT, said policy attention has shifted from building computing facilities to whether resources can be perceived, scheduled and ultimately used by enterprises and industries. China is carrying out special initiatives to empower small and medium-sized enterprises with inclusive computing power, exploring service models such as computing supermarkets and computing banks, lowering the threshold for SMEs and pushing computing resources into the real economy. In the next stage, he said, the focus will be not only on building resources, but also on connecting resources, networks, applications and services. Zhong Zhihong, chief engineer of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, said the next step is to strengthen systematic planning, improve computing utilization efficiency and accelerate building a multilevel, tiered computing architecture. The ministry will continue improving coordinated monitoring and efficient use of computing resources. It will also strengthen computing-network integration, build high-speed, low-latency and resilient transmission channels, deploy city-level millisecond access on demand and advance construction of computing interoperability nodes, Zhong said. China will invest a cumulative 3.8 trillion yuan ($566 billion) in information infrastructure by end-2030 and boost its intelligent computing power to 9,800 EFLOPS, according to a new industry blueprint unveiled by the MIIT last week. The 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period for the information and communications sector — officially published on Monday — sets a clear roadmap for high-quality development over the next five years, focusing on five priorities: consolidating infrastructure, improving public services, optimizing governance, mitigating risks and expanding opening-up. Chen Yangfan, general manager of China Mobile, said the company will focus on heterogeneous interconnectivity, cross-domain scheduling and model services, accelerate research and development and application of key generic computing technologies, and achieve full-stack domestic innovation from chips to models. It will also deepen capital coordination and strategic investment in artificial intelligence and chip companies. China Mobile is building stronger computing infrastructure with a moderately advanced approach. It is building AI data centers, aligning with the national "east data, west computing" project, and deploying gigawatt-level data parks. Its AI data centers contracted scale exceeds 7 GW. CAICT, together with partners such as Huawei, recently released the 2026 Storage Development Report, which showed that by end-June, China's total data storage capacity reached 2,021 exabytes, up 11 percent year-on-year. Advanced storage accounted for 32 percent, exceeding 640 EB. Regional storage development is becoming more intensive and coordinated, with imbalances improving. China's storage industry has entered a new cycle of simultaneous scale expansion and quality upgrading. masi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Probe starts into Qingdao shipyard fire
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Probe starts into Qingdao shipyard fire State Council launches an investigation to trace cause after deadly blaze killed 25 The State Council, China's Cabinet, has launched an investigation into the major fire that occurred at a shipyard in Qingdao, Shandong province, on Thursday, killing 25 people and injuring five, the Ministry of Emergency Management announced on Monday. A State Council investigation team, led by the ministry, held its first plenary meeting on Monday. The meeting set out the investigation plan and called for investigators to identify the cause of the accident as soon as possible. Before the meeting began, all the participants observed a moment of silence for the victims of the accident. Song Yuanming, deputy director of the Office of the State Council Work Safety Committee and vice-minister of emergency management, chaired the meeting. The investigation will not only examine the cause of the fire, but also determine whether the shipyard, industry supervision and local authorities had acted responsibly. Those found responsible for the accident will be held accountable in accordance with the law, the announcement said. The inquiry will follow the principles of scientific rigor, compliance with laws and regulations, seeking truth from facts and focusing on practical results. The authorities were also urged to draw broader lessons from the accident. Local governments, relevant departments and centrally administered State-owned enterprises were told to strengthen workplace safety and step up inspections for fire hazards. Investigators will also pay particular attention to subcontracting and illegal practices connected with it. The meeting called for wider safety checks in sectors including hazardous chemicals, mining, industry and trade, transportation, construction and special equipment, in an effort to prevent serious accidents. The fire broke out at around 11:15 am on Thursday aboard a foreign cargo vessel undergoing repairs at China State Shipbuilding Corporation Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding Co. Authorities have not yet disclosed the nationality of the vessel or of those killed or injured. There were 42 people aboard the vessel when the fire broke out. Twelve managed to evacuate, while 30 others were trapped. The blaze was extinguished at around 2:30 pm. Provincial and Qingdao authorities immediately activated emergency response mechanisms, mobilizing emergency management, fire and rescue, public security, health and industry bodies to carry out rescue operations. By 7:24 pm that day, the search and rescue operation had concluded, with all 30 trapped people found. The five injured were taken to hospital, where they remain in stable condition, while 25 were confirmed dead. Experts specializing in fire investigations from five provincial-level regions arrived at the site early on Friday to conduct preliminary inspections and analysis. The investigation team includes representatives from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Transport, the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council, the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, the National Fire and Rescue Administration and the Shandong provincial government. Officials from relevant departments of the Communist Party of China Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Commission of Supervision, as well as the Supreme People's Procuratorate, attended the meeting. yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China opposes Japan's joint military exercise
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
China opposes Japan's joint military exercise A Chinese Defense Ministry spokesman on Monday voiced opposition to a joint military exercise involving Japan, the United States and Australia, as well as Japan's forward deployment of long-range offensive weapons, saying such moves increase the risk of military confrontation in the region. Jiang Bin, spokesman for the Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks in response to reports that Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force is conducting a joint exercise, dubbed "Oriental Shield 26", with the US and Australian armies in Hokkaido and Kagoshima from Sept 8 to 24. The US Typhon mid-range missile system will participate in the exercise for the first time, according to reports, raising concerns among countries in the region. Jiang said the exercise is being used to advance the deployment of long-range offensive weapons under the guise of a "shield", undermining the security interests of other countries and increasing the risk of an arms race and military confrontation in the region, thereby posing a serious threat to regional peace and stability. "We firmly oppose this," Jiang said. On Aug 31, Russia lodged a protest with the Japanese embassy in Russia over the joint military exercise. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said on Sept 1 that deploying such weapons on Japanese territory, including under the pretext of military exercises, would threaten Russia's security and was "absolutely unacceptable" to Moscow. Russia would take countermeasures to ensure its national defense and security, she said. China has also repeatedly expressed opposition to the deployment of US mid-range missile systems in Asian countries. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a news conference in May that China firmly opposes such deployments and has repeatedly expressed its concerns over the issue. The Typhon missile system is a strategically offensive weapon that undermines the legitimate security interests of other countries, threatens regional strategic security and increases the risk of military confrontation and an arms race, Guo said. "It does nothing to promote regional peace and stability and is detrimental in every respect," Guo said. Jiang also pointed out that Japan has repeatedly breached the principles of its pacifist constitution and its exclusively defense-oriented policy by developing long-range offensive weapons and stepping up its military activities overseas. He criticized Japan's military expansion as moving toward a new form of militarism, saying it caters to the interests of countries outside the region while encouraging bloc confrontation and increasing tensions. "Any move that fuels Japan's military ambitions will only plunge the region into a dangerous vortex and will eventually bring harm to the country itself," Jiang said. He urged the countries concerned to respect the security concerns of other countries, correct their erroneous practices and contribute positively to regional peace and stability through concrete actions. lishangyi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China sets out road map for smarter, greener vehicles
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
China sets out road map for smarter, greener vehicles China has set out a five-year policy road map to enable the widespread use of automated-driving vehicles by 2030, while accelerating the shift toward electrification, reduced energy consumption and safer, intelligent mobility in the automotive industry. According to a plan for the development of the intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, released on Friday by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and eight other government departments, new energy vehicles are expected to account for 70 percent of new passenger vehicle sales and 40 percent of new commercial vehicle sales in China by 2030. The plan also aims to establish China as a global automotive powerhouse. Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Association, said that these targets reflect market potential as well as a phased development strategy. "China's new energy passenger vehicle retail penetration rate has already exceeded 60 percent, providing a realistic foundation for an increase to 70 percent over five years," said Cui. According to the association, NEVs accounted for a record 65.2 percent of domestic passenger vehicle retail sales in August, up 9.9 percentage points from a year earlier. Given the current situation, the target of 40 percent for commercial vehicles is a more pragmatic one, as the adoption of NEVs remains weak on long-haul routes and charging and refueling networks still need to be developed further, Cui added. He said the strategy is to establish passenger vehicles as a benchmark while allocating resources to address weaknesses in the commercial vehicle sector. The plan also sets more stringent energy-efficiency goals. By 2030, the average fuel consumption of new passenger vehicles is targeted at 3.3 liters per 100 kilometers, and average electricity consumption for new battery electric passenger vehicles is set at 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 100 km. Zhang Xiang, a visiting professor at Huanghe Science and Technology University, said that the targets will encourage car manufacturers to produce smaller and lighter vehicles. "Models failing to meet the mandatory energy consumption standards will not be included in the MIIT's product catalog," Zhang said. "This signals a shift in the industry's development logic from scale expansion to high-quality growth driven by energy conservation and carbon reduction," he added. In the field of intelligent driving, the plan aims to promote "highly automated" driving on expressways, urban express roads, and some city streets by 2030. It also seeks to accelerate the development of automotive-specific artificial intelligence models, build high-value scenario libraries for automated driving, and expand the use of AI technologies in vehicles. With regard to the industry, the plan aims to increase labor productivity by 15 percent from 2025 levels, strengthen Chinese brands, establish globally leading automakers and suppliers, and ensure a carbon emissions peak for the auto industry before 2030. From an automaker's perspective, BYD said the plan provides systematic and strategic guidance by defining the industry's overall goals, core priorities and implementation path for the next five years. "It sets higher standards for innovation, the competitive landscape, compliance and international expansion, while responding directly to current industry challenges and companies' operational needs," the company said, adding that it would maintain a high level of R&D investment and focus increasingly on key areas such as electrification and intelligent vehicle technologies. lijiaying@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Single solution to rise of 'solo economy'
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Single solution to rise of 'solo economy' More Chinese are choosing to live alone, reshaping spending and tourism habits Xia Xiaosen, a 39-year-old content creator from Dalian, Liaoning province, who lives alone, prefers to buy fewer items but spend more on quality goods. One of her biggest monthly household expenses is her beloved cat Statham. When she left the comfort of the family home five years ago, she soon discovered that greater independence came with a price tag. Setting up a household from scratch meant buying furniture, appliances and household items, something she had never thought about before. Living alone also changed the way she viewed money. Managing household expenses and daily chores encouraged her to budget more carefully and purchase with greater focus. Rather than buying in bulk, she now chooses smaller quantities of higher quality goods. For instance, she prefers a small box of fresh strawberries over a large bag of budget-friendly fruit. "I don't need large quantities. I prefer fresh, high-quality food that suits my pace. That is what the solo economy means to me: buying less, but better," said Xia. Smart home devices have become essential to her daily routine. A robot vacuum, a dishwasher and automated pet care tools help her manage household chores more efficiently. Her cat is central to her home life and one of her biggest expenses, costing about 400 yuan ($59.60) a month, excluding larger purchases such as an automatic litter box. But she believes the feline companionship is worth the cost. "Living with an animal shows you your own character. It reveals who you really are," she said. A growing number of young Chinese are choosing to live alone or travel independently, giving rise to the "solo economy" centered on one-person consumption. As businesses increasingly adapt products and services to individual consumers, greater autonomy and convenience have come with higher costs and everyday trade-offs. Data from China's Ministry of Civil Affairs shows that the number of marriage registrations fell from 13.47 million couples in 2013 to 6.76 million in 2025. The ministry's Civil Affairs Statistics for the first quarter of 2026 reported 1.697 million registrations, down 6.2 percent year-on-year, continuing the long-term decline. Beike Research Institute's New Era of Solo Living Report estimates that China's "solo-living population" reached 123 million in 2024 and is projected to rise to 150-200 million by 2030. Xia said a solitary life is not without challenges. When she is ill is when she feels the absence of another person most acutely, as she has to deal with everything on her own. She shares her independent lifestyle on social media, and sometimes receives hostile comments questioning why a woman would choose to live alone. "There is still a bias. Some people cannot accept that a woman living independently can feel fulfilled," she said. But living alone has expanded her social life in unexpected ways. When traveling, she often chooses hostels because they make it easier to meet new people. Her attitude toward doing things on her own has also changed. She once felt self-conscious about going to concerts or the cinema alone, but now sees those experiences as liberating. "I used to think doing things alone looked sad. Now I go to a concert by myself and end up meeting other people who came alone too. It feels free," she said.

item.title: Chinese e-bikes power worldwide shift in urban mobility
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
"The best thing about having an electric bike is that you just go past people," said a reviewer of DYU, an e-bike brand based in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, in an Instagram video. "Put it on high assist, and it helps with the pedaling. You can take the hills, miss all the crowds. It's a dream ride." That feeling of effortless mobility is one reason why e-bikes are reshaping urban transportation and why Chinese manufacturers are rapidly expanding overseas. China was once known as the "bicycle kingdom", when bikes were used by Chinese residents as the most common means of transportation. Today, it is becoming the world's e-bike powerhouse. Walk along the canals of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, through the streets of Munich in Germany or on the greenways of Portland, Oregon, in the United States, and bikes are hard to miss. In 2025, Chinese manufacturers exported 26.7 million electric two-wheelers worth a total of $6.829 billion. At the center of that growth was the electric bicycle — a machine that looks much like a traditional bicycle but pairs pedals with sensors, a battery and a quiet electric motor, transforming steep bridges and long commutes into manageable rides. For many riders, the appeal goes beyond convenience. Studies show that e-bikes encourage more people to cycle regularly, particularly older adults and those with limited mobility or knee pain. "This isn't just a bike with a battery," said Lu Jinlong, honorary chairman of the Jiangsu Bicycle and Electric Vehicle Association. "It's a response to how people want to live — healthier, greener and less dependent on cars." The market reflects that shift. The number of e-bike brands in the US doubled from about 100 in 2021 to roughly 200 by 2022, with most of the new entrants being Chinese companies. In Southeast Asia, rising fuel prices and worsening traffic congestion are also accelerating demand for electric two-wheelers. According to the US-based business consulting company Frost & Sullivan, Europe's e-bike market was worth 15 billion euros ($17.3 billion) in 2024 and is projected to grow to 21.2 billion euros by 2029. Globally, Fortune Business Insights expects the market to grow from $50.14 billion in 2024 to $148.7 billion by 2032. While Chinese consumers have largely embraced low-cost electric scooters for short-distance travel, European cities offer something different: extensive cycling infrastructure, government subsidies and a deeply rooted cycling culture. The region thus became an ideal testing ground for premium electric bicycles. That opportunity drew Shenzhen entrepreneur Liang Xiaoling into the European market. In 2021, Liang founded TENWAYS with a simple idea: combining China's manufacturing efficiency with European design and software-driven intelligence. Backed by investors including Hillhouse, Tencent and L Catterton, TENWAYS now sells more than 96 percent of its e-bikes to Europe and is gearing up for what could become Hong Kong's first public listing by a pure-play e-bike company. Its flagship commuter model has sold more than 50,000 units in just four years. Between 2022 and 2024, TENWAYS became the fastest-growing e-bike brand in Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, capturing 5.9 percent of the urban commuting segment. Its e-bikes retail for between 1,299 and 4,999 euros, positioning the company firmly in the premium e-bike market. Behind that premium branding lies China's greatest competitive advantage: its manufacturing ecosystem. Industrial clusters across the Pearl River Delta and Yangtze River Delta produce nearly every major component — from frames and motors to batteries, sensors and electronic control systems — allowing companies to shorten development cycles while controlling costs. In November, Chinese e-bike maker Urtopia acquired the US heritage e-bike brand Pedego — a sign that Chinese companies are also using acquisitions to secure brand equity in Western markets. For Chinese companies, the challenge is no longer proving that Chinese brands can build premium e-bikes, but sustaining innovation in a fast-growing market where technology, design and brand recognition are becoming just as important as manufacturing scale.

item.title: As Mid-Autumn Festival nears, mooncakes return
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
Ding Shumin, a Beijing native in her 60s, stood at the counter of a pastry shop in Beijing, carefully selecting mooncakes. One for herself, another for a relative, a few for friends — and some for her grandson. By the time she left the shop, Ding had packed about 20. She could have chosen chocolate, durian and some other contemporary flavors. Instead, she stuck to the taste she has loved since childhood: wuren, a traditional filling made with nuts and seeds. "When I was little, eating mooncakes was one of the things I looked forward to most at Mid-Autumn Festival," Ding said. "Wuren was always my favorite. Even now, I still have to buy some." The packaging of the mooncakes invoked as much nostalgia as the taste. Five mooncakes were first bundled in brown kraft paper, then wrapped in bright red paper bearing the shop's name and the flavor in black calligraphy, before being tied with coarse twine. There was no elaborate gift box — just a humble wrapping that has survived from another era. With Mid-Autumn Festival around the corner on Sept 25, old-fashioned mooncakes are a familiar sight in Beijing, and bakeries are competing for attention with their increasingly inventive flavors. For Li Baozhi, who is in his 50s, has been in the trade for decades and now works with the pastry shop of Ya'er Liji, a time-honored halal food brand known for traditional Beijing flavors, the appeal of the traditional varieties lies in their simplicity. Li began learning to make mooncakes when he was about 20 years old. He remembers the earliest versions as plain, firm and crumbly. "The oldest style may have been made simply with sugar, oil and flour," Li said. "You put the mooncake into a square mold, pressed it flat, knocked it out of the mold and then baked it." Today, Li makes traditional fillings including wuren, black sesame, red bean and jujube paste, which he said are most popular among buyers. The pastry is also distinctly different from the soft, syrupy crust of Cantonese-style mooncakes. "Cantonese-style mooncakes feature a lot of filling and thin skin, while Beijing-style ones have thicker, crispy skin and less filling," Li said. Wuren, he added, is particularly popular among older customers. But preserving tradition does not mean freezing it in time. "Although it is traditional, it still has to be improved. Otherwise, it won't work," he said. For Li, mooncakes are part of the rhythm of everyday Chinese life — much like dumplings at Spring Festival and zongzi, or sticky rice dumplings, during Dragon Boat Festival. A mooncake that costs just a few yuan can carry more meaning than an expensive gift box, he noted. That down-to-earth quality may be precisely what gives traditional mooncakes staying power. In the past, mooncakes were a precious seasonal treat because food was less abundant. Today, they have to compete with a seemingly endless menu of alternatives — including flavors that earlier generations could hardly have imagined. "The sales were even stronger in the past, because there was less choice," Li said. "But now people have more options — you can eat mooncakes, or hairy crabs instead." Yet the ritual has proved difficult to replace. At the bakery where customer Ding shopped, several thousand mooncakes are sold daily, according to Ding Shilong, the restaurant's culinary director. At the busiest point before the festival, sales can climb to 10,000 or even 20,000 pieces a day. In nearby Qianmen, a historic district in central Beijing, 53-year-old Zhai Guangjun runs another traditional bakery tucked inside a hutong. He started selling mooncakes about a month before the festival, with most customers coming from the neighborhood. For many, Zhai said, buying old-fashioned mooncakes is less about novelty than memory — a small edible link to childhood and to the annual promise of family reunions. Mooncake fillings vary widely across China, from Beijing's traditional wuren and jujube pastes to Shanghai's savory fresh meat fillings and the rich lotus seed paste in Guangdong province. The same tension between tradition and novelty plays out elsewhere in China too. On Sept 8, Russian influencer Marina Maloy, who lives in Shanghai, posted a video of herself sampling mooncakes on Nanjing East Road. Alongside the city's classic fresh meat mooncakes, she tried newer versions flavored with fermented red bean curd sauce, shrimp and crab roe (the rich, golden substance found inside a crab). After sampling her way through the mooncakes, Maloy said the experience gave her a glimpse of people's "respect for tradition and their love of life".

item.title: US expert's 20-year front-row seat to Beijing Xiangshan Forum's rise
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
US expert's 20-year front-row seat to Beijing Xiangshan Forum's rise David Finkelstein, a Distinguished Research Fellow at the Center for Naval Analyses of the United States, shared his reflections on nearly two decades of participation in the Beijing Xiangshan Forum in a recent video posted on the forum's official X account (@XiangshanForum). Finkelstein has been a regular participant in the forum since its inception in 2006, missing only two editions. He said the Beijing Xiangshan Forum has been one of the highlights of his annual conference schedule and that he looks forward to returning to Beijing for this year's event. Over the past 20 years, Finkelstein said he has witnessed the forum grow from a small gathering of scholars into a major international event. For Finkelstein, one of the most important things he has gained from the forum is the opportunity to interact with scholars from around the world. Participants from Europe, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and North America can gather to discuss pressing issues of the day at the forum, which gives him a valuable opportunity to reconnect with former colleagues and longtime friends in China, he said. Finkelstein said he looks forward to returning to Beijing this autumn and seeing friends from China and around the world.

item.title: BRICS paves the way and the Global South has its say
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-12
BRICS paves the way and the Global South has its say Share - WeChat
The 18th BRICS Summit kicks off in New Delhi. Standing at the forefront of the Global South, BRICS represents nearly half of the world's population and about one-third of global GDP. Amid rising protectionism, BRICS offers a broad platform for openness, inclusiveness, and win-win cooperation.
